tooltips.optimizer: Adam for ResNet (proven fine-tuning baseline). AdamW for ConvNeXt and DINOv2 — decoupled weight decay prevents overfitting on small datasets.
tooltips.learning_rate: Fine-tuning LR from the model registry. ResNet: 0.001 (standard), ConvNeXt: 0.0001 (LayerNorm is sensitive to large gradients), DINOv2: 0.0002 (LoRA adapter).
tooltips.weight_decay: L2 regularization strength. 0 for ResNet (BatchNorm provides implicit regularization), 0.05 for ConvNeXt (ConvNeXt paper recipe), 0.01 for DINOv2 (light regularization on LoRA adapters).
tooltips.patience: Stops training after 15 consecutive epochs without val_loss improvement. Catches convergence without premature stopping.
tooltips.batch_size: Physical batch=8 (fits 4GB VRAM). Effective batch=32 via gradient accumulation (4 steps). Mathematically identical to batch=32 for cross-entropy loss.
tooltips.epochs: Maximum training duration. Early stopping terminates earlier via patience.
tooltips.test_accuracy: Overall fraction of correctly classified test images (300 total, 50 per class).
tooltips.f1_macro: Harmonic mean of per-class F1 scores. Preferred over accuracy for imbalanced datasets.

research.hero_title: Ultra-Fine-Grained Classification and Open-Set Recognition of Ophrys Orchids
research.hero_university: University of Naples Federico II — DIETI — Master's Degree in Computer Science
research.intro_p1_mid: includes over 300 species of European orchids characterized by an extraordinary morphological similarity that makes their taxonomic identification extremely complex even for expert botanists. This difficulty, known as ultra-fine-grained classification (UFGVC)
research.intro_p1_after: , represents a significant challenge for computer vision systems.
research.intro_p2_before: This thesis addresses the problem by systematically comparing six architectures (ResNet, ConvNeXt, DINOv2) across three learning paradigms: cross-entropy, supervised contrastive learning (SupCon)
research.contrib_1: Multi-architecture benchmark across three learning paradigms
research.contrib_2: Curated dataset: 2,192 training images and 300 test images, 6 species with MD5 deduplication, and O. garganica used as the hidden novel class for open-set evaluation
research.contrib_3: Latent space analysis via t-SNE projections
research.contrib_4: Open-set evaluation with Mahalanobis, KNN, and Energy techniques
research.dataset_caption: Image distribution per species in training and test splits. O. garganica is in training for Studio I-A–I-C and excluded from training in Studio II-A, where it is reserved for testing as the novel class.
research.dataset_intro: The dataset comprises images of six taxonomic entities of the O. sphegodes complex, all photographed in Italian territory, mainly in Apulia and on the Gargano. Images come from two sources: field photographs taken by the researchers constitute the primary source for O. majellensis and O. sphegodes Palena (species with no counterpart in databases); images collected from open internet databases cover the four most common species: O. exaltata, O. garganica, O. incubacea and O. sphegodes.
research.dataset_callout_leakage: In the preliminary phases (pre-renumbering), the dataset presented a critical data leakage problem: binary-duplicate (MD5) images appeared in both training and test sets under different filenames. The discovery was made via MD5 content hashing. Starting from Studio I-A, the dataset was cleaned using a three-phase protocol: (1) MD5 deduplication, (2) extraction of a balanced hold-out of 50 images per class, (3) stratified 5-fold cross-validation with seed 57. This split forms the basis of all experiments.
research.dataset_callout_novel: O. garganica, recognized as a distinct entity of the O. sphegodes complex, is excluded from training in Studio II-A and reserved exclusively for the test set as a novel class never seen during training. Its taxonomic relevance makes it a challenging case study for evaluating known/novel separability at ultra-fine granularity.
research.dataset_preprocessing: Raw images are processed by a pre-trained Faster R-CNN object detection module that automatically crops the flower by removing the background. Letterbox resize preserves the original aspect ratio with black padding. Input sizes are architecture-native: 256×512 for ResNet, 224×224 for ConvNeXt and DINOv2. During cross-validation, minority classes are oversampled through augmentations (rotations, flip, color jitter, cutout).
research.sect_exp4: Studio II-A — SpHOR with Hidden Novel Class
research.sect_exp5: Studio II-B — SpHOR with 2 Hidden Novel Classes
research.metodo_exp5: Same protocol (SupCon + SpHOR, two phases), but O. garganica and O. majellensis are excluded from training, leaving four known classes (1,477 images). Closed-set F1 is measured on 200 images, OSR/GCD on the full 300-image pool.
research.exp5_motivazione: Studio II-A tests open-set recognition with a single hidden novel class. Studio II-B stresses the system further: two species are hidden from training, halving the known world to four classes. Training uses 1,477 images; closed-set evaluation reports test F1 on the four known classes (200 images); OSR and GCD operate on the full test pool (300 images: 200 known + 100 novel).
research.exp5_caption: Studio II-B — Cross-validation and test F1 on the four known classes (n=200, 5-fold means). All hold: DINOv2-Base 0.930 ± 0.004, ConvNeXt-Tiny 0.923 ± 0.009, DINOv2-Small 0.923 ± 0.007.
research.exp5_subs_osr: Open-Set Recognition with Two Novel Classes
research.exp5_osr: Embedding-based detectors hold with two hidden novels (ConvNeXt-Tiny Mahalanobis 0.849, Ensemble 0.843), while the logit-based Energy detector degrades systematically (down to 0.410).
research.exp5_osr_caption: Studio II-B — OSR AUROC per detector (4 known vs 2 novel, n=200+100). Ensemble* is a supplement (rank average, equal weights 1/3, no tuning).
research.exp5_gcd: With standard SS-KMeans, discovery of the two novel classes stays near chance (ACC new 0.12–0.38), while NMI remains stable (0.918–0.947): the partition structure is preserved even when novels are not isolated.
research.exp5_delong: DeLong 95% CIs accompany every AUROC; the paired KNN comparison between the two best architectures gives parity (p=0.9766), while in Studio II-A KNN beats Energy (+0.110, p=0.0015).
research.metodo_disegno_intro: The experiments are organized into five series, each adding methodological complexity to the previous one, in a path from closed classification to the open world:
research.metodo_exp1: all architectures are trained with CE loss for 150 epochs with early stopping (patience 15). Establishes the closed-set performance baseline.
research.metodo_exp2: introduces two-phase training. Phase 1: backbone + projection head (128-dim) trained with SupConLoss (τ=0.07) for 100 epochs, validated with 1-NN accuracy. Phase 2: frozen backbone, linear classifier trained with CE for 50 epochs.
research.metodo_exp3: like Studio I-B but with spherical orthogonal prototypes (SpHOR): a SupCon-only warm-up (20 epochs), then one unit prototype per class initialised on the class centroid, then the hybrid loss SupCon + w·vMF + 0.01·L_rep, with w growing linearly 0→1 over 20 epochs and hard vMF assignment (κ=10). At test time, four OSR detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) determine whether a sample is known or novel.
research.metodo_exp4: identical to Studio I-C but with O. garganica excluded from training: five known classes, garganica reserved for testing as the novel class for OSR and NCD evaluation.
research.metodo_validazione: All experiments use stratified 5-fold cross-validation with seed 57. The main metric for closed-set classification is macro F1, robust to the natural class imbalance (152 images for O. majellensis vs 563 for O. garganica). For open-set, AUROC is used: it measures the system's ability to discriminate known vs novel samples across all thresholds.
research.metodo_pipeline_osr: For OSR evaluation, the model trained on five known classes is tested on a set that includes O. garganica as the unknown class. The procedure consists of three phases: (1) embedding extraction from training and test sets via a frozen backbone; (2) training of four detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) on known embeddings only; (3) computation of AUROC.
research.metodo_arch_fig_caption: Diagram of the training and evaluation pipeline: from image collection to result publication.
research.metodo_osr_flow_caption: Open-Set Recognition pipeline: embedding extraction, detector training, novelty detection. The detectors evaluate the distance/probability that a sample belongs to a known class.

The hardest species (O. sphegodes, O. garganica) show the most marked drop when moving to contrastive paradigms.

research.contesto_p1_after: (Orchidaceae) includes terrestrial orchids widespread throughout the Mediterranean basin. The plants are perennial, with basal rosette leaves and a flowering stem producing 2 to 12 flowers. Each flower is characterized by a large velvety labellum that constitutes the most conspicuous and diagnostic morphological element.
research.contesto_p2_mid: are known for their pollination system based on sexual mimicry (pseudocopulation)
research.contesto_p2_after: . Each species produces a unique blend of allomones that mimics the sex pheromone of a specific pollinator species. The labellum, in shape, color, and texture, visually mimics the female insect's body; the speculum — a reflective spot on the labellum — simulates light reflected from wings. Only about 10% of flowers are actually pollinated, but each produces up to 12,000 seeds.
research.contesto_p3_mid1: is one of the most taxonomically controversial groups in the plant kingdom
research.contesto_p3_mid2: . Estimates of the number of species vary dramatically: from about 20 (
research.contesto_p3_mid3: , 1980) to over 130 (Delforge, 1995). Frequent hybridization produces over 250 described natural hybrids, and molecular studies have revealed heterogeneous copies of ribosomal ITS DNA in single individuals. The
research.contesto_p3_mid4: complex (the "forretterelle") is one of the most variable groups, with at least 18 subspecific taxa.
research.contesto_p4_before: Our dataset adopts an intermediate classification, treating six entities —
research.contesto_p4_after: — as distinct species, consistent with the Italian taxonomic tradition. The Gargano peninsula constitutes a diversity hotspot for the complex.
research.arch_before: Six architectures from three families were selected to cover the state of the art in visual classification. Classic convolutional networks
research.arch_mid3: were chosen as baselines for computational efficiency. Modernized CNNs
research.arch_mid6: incorporate Transformer design choices (7×7 kernel, Layer Normalization, GELU). The Vision Transformers
research.arch_after: are pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on 142 million images.
research.exp1_p1_before: Studio I-A establishes the closed-set classification baseline with standard CE loss. The softmax objective separates classes with decision hyperplanes but does not structure the latent space: two samples of the same species can project into arbitrary regions of space, as long as the classifier assigns them to the correct class. This lack of structure is acceptable for closed-set classification but becomes critical in open-world scenarios
research.exp1_fig_caption: Training and validation curves for DINOv2-Base in Studio I-A (CE), averaged over the 5 folds. Training loss converges toward 0 while validation reaches its minimum in the early epochs and then plateaus, indicating an overfitting regime typical of cross-entropy on small datasets.
research.exp2_p1_before: To address the structural limitation of CE, Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) is adopted
research.exp2_p1_after: . The SupCon loss explicitly attracts samples of the same class and repels those of different classes in L2-normalized space. The result is a metric space where cosine distance reflects semantic similarity — an essential property for open-set recognition and novel class discovery
research.exp2_fig2_caption: Per-species F1 for the best model of each experiment (Studio I-A: ResNet-50, Studio I-B and Studio I-C: DINOv2-Base). O. sphegodes is systematically the most difficult species; O. majellensis the easiest.
research.exp2_fig3_caption: Training and validation curves for DINOv2-Small during SupCon training.
research.benchmark_intro: The following table consolidates the performance of all architectures across the experiments, for closed-set classification (test F1), open-set (AUROC) and unsupervised clustering (NMI).
research.futuri_li1: Dataset expansion via citizen science and generative AI.
research.futuri_li3: Systematic integration of XAI with validation by expert botanists.
research.futuri_li4: Field validation through deployment of the OrchID OSR application.
research.risultati_li1_before: Closed-set champion: ResNet-50 + CE in Studio I-A (F1 0.884 ± 0.009); best among contrastive paradigms is DINOv2-Base
research.risultati_li1_mid: + SupCon (F1 0.808 ± 0.032) — best trade-off among contrastive paradigms.
research.risultati_li2_mid: + SpHOR (AUROC 0.875, novel O. garganica) — demonstration that OSR is achievable in ultra-FGVC.
research.risultati_li3: Open-set recognition goes from a failure with SupCon (known accuracy 0.0) to AUROC 0.875 with SpHOR in Studio II-A.
research.risultati_li4: Unsupervised clustering recovers species for high-capacity models, confirming the quality of the SpHOR metric space.
research.risultati_li5: Uninformed K-means isolates the novel only on DINOv2-Base (ACC new 0.83 ± 0.03, NMI 0.79).
research.exp1_training: All six architectures were trained for a maximum of 150 epochs with patience 15 for early stopping, using the recipes defined in the configuration table.
research.exp1_risultati_before: The table reports F1 scores (5-fold means, test 300). ResNet-50 reaches the highest test F1 (0.884 ± 0.009), followed by ResNet-18 (0.847 ± 0.016) and DINOv2-Base (0.764 ± 0.058). ConvNeXt models remain lower (0.687 ± 0.032 and 0.513 ± 0.164) with wide variance for ConvNeXt-S (±0.164). DINOv2-S (0.695 ± 0.041) underperforms validation. The CV-test gap is negative for all models: the official test is harder than validation.
research.exp1_risultati_mid: phenomenon: with approximately 2,200 training samples, ResNets (11–25M parameters) operate in the over-parameterized regime where generalization improves with model size, while ConvNeXt-Small (50M parameters) lies closer to the interpolation threshold where overfitting is more severe.
research.exp1_risultati_after: The gap tends to increase with model parameters for the ConvNeXt and DINOv2 families, while ResNets show stable or positive generalization thanks to the implicit regularization of batch normalization.
research.exp1_embedding: The t-SNE projection of DINOv2-Small embeddings reveals that CE produces a poorly structured latent space. Although species are approximately separable, considerable overlap is observed between morphologically similar taxa — particularly between O. sphegodes and O. garganica, which belong to the same taxonomic complex. This lack of geometric structure is intrinsic to the softmax objective: the model has no incentive to organize the latent space beyond what is necessary for classification, producing representations inadequate for open-set recognition. The cosine silhouette score confirms this quantitatively: ResNet-18 achieves 0.664 (CE); with SpHOR, ConvNeXt-Tiny (0.565), ConvNeXt-Small (0.534) and ResNet-50 (0.546) show the strongest separation, followed by DINOv2-Small (0.281) and DINOv2-Base (0.191).
research.exp1_fig_cv_gap: Generalization gap (Test F1 − CV F1) as a function of model parameters. Positive values indicate the model generalizes beyond the cross-validation estimate; negative values indicate overfitting. Modern architectures (ConvNeXt, DINOv2) show larger gaps than ResNets, consistent with the double descent phenomenon.
research.exp2_protocollo: A two-phase training procedure was employed. In Phase 1, the backbone and a projection head (embedding dimension → 128) were trained using the SupCon loss with temperature τ = 0.07. Validation was performed via 1-nearest neighbor accuracy on frozen backbone embeddings. In Phase 2, the projection head was removed and a linear classifier was trained on the frozen backbone using cross-entropy for 50 epochs. Freezing the backbone in Phase 2 is a fundamental methodological choice: it preserves the metric structure of the embedding space, preventing the classifier from distorting representations to maximize closed-set accuracy at the expense of open-set separability.
research.exp2_risultati: The table presents results (5-fold means). DINOv2-Base achieved the highest test F1 (0.808 ± 0.032, gap −0.125). DINOv2-Small (0.710 ± 0.029, gap −0.204) remains competitive. Large ConvNeXt and ResNet underperform in SupCon.
research.exp2_overfitting_detail: ConvNeXt-Small shows the largest negative CV-test gap (−0.254); DINOv2-Base gap −0.125, ResNet-50 −0.028: on the official test all models generalize worse than in validation.
research.exp2_embedding_osr: The t-SNE projection shows that SupCon produces markedly more cohesive clusters than CE. Intra-class variance is reduced and inter-class separation is improved, particularly for the most distinctive species (O. exaltata, O. incubacea). However, an open-set evaluation reveals a critical limitation: the detector showed 0.0 accuracy on known classes at all thresholds, classifying all inputs as unknown. The worst (ResNet-18) stops at 0.485, near chance; the six-model mean is 0.575. This indicates that although SupCon produces well-separated class clusters, the distances between clusters are not significantly larger than intra-cluster distances — a fundamental limitation when inter-class morphological differences are as subtle as they are in ultra-fine-grained domains. The embedding space lacks the angular margin needed to distinguish "familiar but unseen" from "truly novel."
research.exp3_motivazione_before: The failure of SupCon-based OSR detection motivated the adoption of Spherical Orthogonal Prototypes (SpHOR)
research.exp3_motivazione_mid: . SpHOR extends contrastive learning with unit prototypes on the sphere, one per class. The representation is trained in two stages: a SupCon-only warm-up, where the classes find their shape, and then the joint phase, where the prototypes are initialised on the class centroids and two terms govern them — the hard vMF assignment, which pulls each image towards the prototype of its own class with a weight growing linearly from 0 to 1, and the squared-cosine repulsion (λ=0.01), which keeps them orthogonal. The prototypes, separated this way, partition the unit sphere into conical regions, each occupied by a single species. At inference time, four detectors evaluate whether a sample belongs to a known class: Mahalanobis distance
research.exp3_motivazione_after: from the nearest prototype, K-nearest neighbors (k=5), Energy score
research.exp3_motivazione_end: , and an Ensemble that combines them via normalized averaging.
research.exp3_closedset: The table reports closed-set metrics (5-fold means). DINOv2-Base leads (0.833 ± 0.031), followed by DINOv2-Small (0.772 ± 0.039) and ResNet-50 (0.719 ± 0.041); ConvNeXt-Tiny drops to 0.710 ± 0.040.
research.exp3_species: The per-species F1 breakdown reveals a coherent pattern for modern architectures. O. sphegodes — the most phenotypically variable taxon — is the most penalized species (F1 0.689 for ConvNeXt-Tiny and 0.738 for DINOv2-Base). Conversely, O. majellensis stays on top (0.761–0.915) as the most morphologically distinctive taxon, while O. sphegodes Palena shows variable performance across architectures (0.390 for ConvNeXt-Tiny, 0.820 for DINOv2-Base). O. exaltata and O. garganica, belonging to Clade G, show intermediate F1 (0.81–0.85). For the ResNets the pattern is more marked: O. incubacea suffers the severest drop for ResNet-18 (F1 0.135, against a mean of 0.442), while O. majellensis and O. sphegodes Palena remain the best classified (0.826 and 0.779).
research.exp4_motivazione: Studio II-A is identical to Studio I-C in protocol (SupCon + SpHOR, two phases), but O. garganica is excluded from training, leaving five known classes. The model is evaluated on the test set that includes the hidden novel class, measuring open-set recognition: four detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) determine whether a sample belongs to a known class or should be classified as unknown.
research.exp4_caption: Studio II-A — Closed-set F1 on five known classes, AUROC and NMI on the novel class.
research.exp4_osr_intro: The OSR evaluation with O. garganica as the hidden novel class yields positive and consistent results across several architectures:
research.exp4_osr_dinov2b: DINOv2-Base reaches the best AUROC (0.875) with the Ensemble detector, confirming that the Vision Transformer representations, combined with orthogonal prototypes, effectively encode the notion of novelty.
research.exp4_osr_convnext: ConvNeXt-Tiny reaches AUROC 0.850: the most balanced configuration between closed-set precision and open-set robustness.
research.exp4_osr_resnet: ResNet-18 remains weak (AUROC 0.507): the limited backbone capacity does not support the geometric structure required for OSR.
research.exp4_osr_ensemble: The Ensemble is the most robust detector, being the best for the three most performant configurations (DINOv2-Base, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ConvNeXt-Small).
research.exp4_osr_auroc_caption: OSR AUROC by architecture in Studio II-A with O. garganica as the novel class (best detector per architecture). DINOv2-Base (0.875) and ConvNeXt-Tiny (0.850) clearly exceed the chance level (0.5); ResNet-18 remains the weakest (0.507).
research.exp4_clustering: Unsupervised clustering on Studio II-A embeddings recovers species for high-capacity models: uninformed K-means (K=6, mean over 10 seeds) discovers the novel class only with DINOv2-Base (ACC new 0.83±0.03, NMI 0.79), while semi-supervised SS-KM preserves the global structure (pool NMI 0.921–0.928). Weaker architectures recover the structure only partially.
research.exp4_tsne_novel_caption: t-SNE projection of Studio II-A embeddings for DINOv2-Base: the five known species (circles) are well separated, while the novel class O. garganica (crosses) sits at the margins of the known clusters, remaining detectable by the open-set detectors.
research.osr_1vs2_caption: OSR comparison between Studio II-A (1 novel) and Studio II-B (2 novels): embedding-based AUROCs hold, Energy degrades in the two-novel scenario.
research.gcd_exp5_caption: GCD novel discovery (ACC new): standard SS-KMeans fails (Studio II-A ≈0, with the ResNet-50 exception at 0.44), uninformed KMeans discovers on DINOv2-Base (0.83); with two novels (Studio II-B) discovery stays low (0.12–0.38) while NMI is stable (≈0.93).
research.sintesi_implicazioni: This study shows that open-set recognition is achievable at ultra-fine granularity: with O. garganica excluded from training, DINOv2-Base with SpHOR reaches AUROC 0.875 in Studio II-A, clearly exceeding the chance level (0.5). Cross-entropy and SupCon alone are instead insufficient for open-world scenarios: CE does not structure the latent space and the SupCon detector fails (known accuracy 0.0). Spherical orthogonal prototypes provide the necessary regularization. Unsupervised clustering recovers species when the metric space is stable (NMI 0.79 in Studio II-A). Confusion matrices reveal systematic patterns: the O. exaltata → O. sphegodes pair is the most frequent error (26% in Studio I-C), consistent with the taxonomy of the O. sphegodes complex, where species share overlapping morphological traits.
research.sintesi_necessita: Discovering new Ophrys species from visual data alone would require additional cues — geographic context, phenological information, or part-based anatomical correspondence as proposed by recent methods such as APL and PartGCD. These methods decompose the visual representation into anatomical parts (labellum, gynostemium, sepals) and align them across species, potentially capturing the fine-grained diagnostic characters that taxonomists use.
research.sintesi_limitazioni: Several limitations should be acknowledged. The open-set evaluation was conducted with one novel species in Studio II-A (O. garganica) and two in Studio II-B (O. garganica + O. majellensis), all belonging to the same taxonomic complex as the known classes. Key AUROC comparisons carry DeLong 95% confidence intervals and paired tests. Results were obtained with full fine-tuning (ResNet/ConvNeXt) and LoRA rank 8 (DINOv2) on a local T2000 GPU. All experiments were conducted on a single dataset with limited geographic coverage (primarily Apulia and Gargano); generalizability to other Mediterranean populations is not guaranteed. Furthermore, the mixed provenance of images (field vs internet photos) introduces a potential domain bias, although all six species have field photos and only four have internet photos. The confusion patterns follow the taxonomy of the complex — O. exaltata ↔ O. sphegodes (16–28%) — indicating that the model learns genuine morphological traits rather than mere domain shortcuts.
